text: One of the inspectors hums. While he looks under the tarp and pretends there is nothing there, he hums. After one visit I found a note under a rope on the rail. A song title, nothing else. I played it the next day. They still come around the point sometimes. He still hums. We never talk about it.
There's a cormorant who sits on my anchor buoy and stares at the wheelhouse. Not at the island. Not at the fish. At me. Gerrit and I disagree about most things... [mutters] we agree about him.

My mug went overboard once. My only mug. I drank coffee out of a tin for a week. Then a fisherman came alongside and handed it up: it came up in his net, with a little crab living in it. I put the crab back, and the mug back on the hook. [sighs] No man overboard.

The shop on the harbour where I buy coffee has an accordion in the window. It's been there for years. Nobody buys it, nobody plays it, nobody asks. I check on it every time I go shopping. One week it was gone, and I rowed home more upset than I have any right to be. Next week it was back. Nobody said a word, and I didn't ask.

The inspectors once boarded the wrong boat. A fishing boat a mile up, with a big aerial on the wheelhouse. They fined him for being a radio station. He came round to me after, very calm, and asked for compensation. Four dedications. Fair, I thought.

A seal got into the dinghy once while I was tied up at the harbour. Lay right across the seat and wouldn't move. I rowed back like that, very carefully, around him. About halfway he just slid over the side and went. Didn't even look back.

Two fishermen had a bet on whether I really exist. One said the station is a tape somebody plays from the shore. The other one rowed over, knocked on the hull twice, said hello Kees, and rowed back. [amused] I heard the money change hands on channel sixteen.

Opa starts on three pulls and a tap with the spanner on the left side of the housing. Always the left. Once I tapped the right, without thinking. [flatly] Took me two days to get him going again. Left side. Always.
I put up a little shaving mirror in the wheelhouse. Gerrit fought it for an hour. Wings out, the full speech. Then he walked off, very upright. I think he thinks he won.

The anchor came up once with a white plastic garden chair around it. Perfectly good chair. For one day this boat had two chairs, and it felt like having visitors. Then I put it back. There's not really room.

There's a coffee machine on the harbour that took two coins off me and gave back nothing. That was years ago. I pass it every supply run. It owes me two coins and an apology, and I'd settle for the apology.
A letter in a bottle, in crayon: do seagulls have teeth? Gerrit got to it first, as usual, so the answer's on the corner of the page. No, they don't. [to Gerrit] You manage.

There's a story on the quay that I used to be famous for something. They heard the bell ring, but they don't know where the clapper hangs. I don't correct them. Most of their versions are better than what really happened.

The inspectors brought a new one once, very young, very serious. While the others were under the tarp he came over and asked, quietly, if I'd sign his clipboard. So I did. Then he wrote me up. [chuckles] Fair enough, really.

Opa ran a whole week once on old oil from the chip shop on the harbour. It works, if you filter it. He ran better than in months. The whole boat smelled of chips, and every gull for miles came to see what was going on. Gerrit chased them all away. [dryly] Best week of his life.

I dropped my reading glasses over the side once, reaching for a rope. For a week I read the record labels with my arms all the way out. Then a fisherman gave me his spare pair. They are a lot stronger than mine. Everything is enormous now. I never gave them back, and he never asked.

I had a toothache out here once for nine days, because I kept thinking it would go away. It didn't. I rowed in, found a dentist, and the girl at the desk asked for my address. I gave her the position of the boat. [amused] She wrote it down. I have no idea if they ever sent a reminder.

The anchor dragged once and I didn't notice. I looked up from a record and the lighthouse was in the wrong window. Two hundred metres, more or less. It took me most of a day to get back to my spot, with Gerrit on the roof watching, like he knew it for hours.

Coming back with the shopping, I missed the ladder and went straight in. Up to my neck. I held the coffee up the whole time. The coffee was fine. The bread was not. I dried it on the roof and ate it anyway. You do, out here.

A listener rowed out once with a cake. Lovely woman. Terrible cake. Very dry, with something in it I still can't name. She waited while I tried it. I ate the whole thing, in four days, and Gerrit would not go near it. [quietly] It was a very kind thing to do.

I cut my own hair out here, with the kitchen scissors and the little mirror. The front went fine. The back I did by feeling. The woman in the harbour shop took one look and said, oh, Kees, and wrote down the number of her niece. I haven't called. It's mostly grown out.

I went into a pub on the harbour once, which I don't really do. Ordered a beer, and the barman looked at me and said, you're the radio. Just from my voice. I said no, people say that a lot. He gave me the beer for free anyway. I didn't argue.

A lad on a jet ski went round and round the boat once, shouting a request. So I put it on, loud, so he could hear it. He was so happy he waved with both hands and fell off. He was fine. He swam back to it singing, I'll give him that.
The woman in the harbour shop keeps the bread from yesterday for me. Every week she asks how Gerrit is, by name. She never once asked how I am. [mutters] I'm starting to take it personally.

Pieter's engine died once, half a mile from here. He drifted over, and I looked through Opa's spare parts and found a fuel filter that fit. It took an hour, with a lot of swearing. He left without a word. The next week there was a box of mackerel on my deck. That's how you say thank you, out here.

A man in a suit rowed out once with a letter for me. Rented rowing boat, shiny shoes, very careful with the oars. He got to about ten metres away and Gerrit went for his hat. He turned around. Never came back. I still feel a bit bad about the hat.

I lost an oar on the way back from shopping once. It just slipped out. I did the rest standing at the back with the other one, waggling it, like I saw in a film. Took two hours. Some kids on the harbour wall cheered every time I went in a circle. [sighs] There were a lot of circles.
